title: paraoxonase 1 polymorphisms and haplotypes and the risk for having offspring affected with spina bifida in southeast mexico
display_name: Paraoxonase 1 polymorphisms and haplotypes and the risk for having offspring affected with spina bifida in Southeast Mexico

authorships.name: Lízbeth González-Herrera
institutions: Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del Instituto Politécnico Nacional

authorships.name: Betzabet Quintanilla‐Vega
institutions: Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del Instituto Politécnico Nacional

abstract: abstract background spina bifida (sb) is a common congenital malformation in southeast mexico. parents of children with sb reside in areas with frequent pesticide spraying or have agriculture activities, suggesting potential exposure to pesticides. paraoxonase 1 ( pon1 ) is the responsible enzyme for deactivation of organophosphates (op) in the central nervous system. polymorphisms of pon1 genes influence the catalytic activity and plasma protein level of the enzyme, therefore, genotypic characterization of pon1 gene represents a potential predictor for susceptibility to op related effects. methods the frequency of pon1 haplotypes and polymorphisms ( 108ct , l55m , and q192r ) were determined in this study. a case control study was performed to evaluate the risk for having offspring affected by sb in 152 cases and 160 control parents. polymorphisms were determined by pcr amplification and restriction fragment length polymorphism and real time pcr. odds ratios and confidence interval 95% were estimated. results genotype frequencies for the three pon1 polymorphisms were distributed according to hardy weinberg expectations ( p > 0.05) and were significantly different between cases and controls ( p < 0.05). the heterozygous ct genotype of 108ct polymorphism, the rr genotype of q192r polymorphism, both lm and mm genotypes of l55m polymorphism, and the haplotypes 221 and 222 (for 108ct , l55m , and q192r ) were associated with the risk for having a child affected by sb ( p < 0.02). the heterozygous 108ct genotype was associated only maternally, whereas the heterozygous l55m genotype was relevant only in the fathers. the rr homozygous genotype was relevant both in mothers and fathers, suggesting the importance of this substrate specific polymorphism. conclusion results suggest that pon1 polymorphisms are relevant risk factors for having offspring affected with sb in this population from southeast mexico. birth defects research (part a), 2010. 2010 wiley liss, inc.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Biochemistry > Enzyme Mechanism

title: high density lipoproteins and atherosclerosis: current concepts
display_name: High‐density lipoproteins and atherosclerosis: current concepts
abstract: dr jim owen described two receptors involved in high density lipoprotein (hdl) homeostasis. high levels of hdl and apoa1 are known to be cardioprotective, but it has only recently been discovered that a low concentration of hdl is itself a risk factor for cardiac events, of roughly equivalent prognostic power as a high concentration of low-density lipoprotein (ldl). the hdl transport pathway moves excess cholesterol from the blood to the liver, where mature hdl particles carrying cholesterol esters bind to liver cells and deliver their load. two recently identified receptors mediate this process. the scavenger receptor class b, type 1, a protein that is abundant on hepatocytes and steroidogenic cells, binds hdl and mediates selective uptake of cholesterol esters. the receptor and the hdl particle are taken into the cell by endocytosis, where the cholesterol esters are hydrolysed and the remaining hdl particle is returned to the circulation. the second efflux receptor was found through studies of hdl deficiency. this is similar to tangier disease, which is characterised by accelerated catabolism of apoa1 and reduced cholesterol efflux to apoa1, and is due to a mutation in the atp-binding cassette transporter, abca1. this shuttles cholesterol across the membrane, making it available to apoa1. the transporter is regulated by phosphorylation, by transcriptional control of its expression and by cholesterol loading via sterol-activated nuclear receptors; the latter are proving interesting drug targets. professor guido franceschini, university of milan, italy professor guido franceschini addressed the cardioprotective actions of hdl. he has investigated the role of hdl in the restoration of coronary flow after plaque rupture and associated reperfusion injury. using an isolated rat heart model, he showed that hdl had a dose-dependent beneficial effect on the speed and volume of restoration of blood flow, whereas ldl had no effect. hdl also reduced the amount of creatine kinase released, indicating that it prevents damage to cardiac myocytes. the major damaging factor in reperfusion injury is tnf-alpha. hdl promotes the efflux of tnf-alpha into the coronary circulation and down-regulates its transcription, blocking the induction that occurs during reperfusion injury. professor franceschini has partially mimicked these effects using synthetic hdl prepared from phospholipids and apoa1 in a rat heart model. this suggests a possible novel therapeutic approach to the preservation of myocardial function after ischaemia/reperfusion injury; however, it is a long way from isolated healthy animal hearts to diseased patient hearts. professor paul durrington, manchester royal infirmary, uk professor paul durrington filled in for bharti mackness, who had taken her husband to hospital after he had completed an unfortunate series of events by damaging his ankle on the way to the conference. the framingham heart study showed a very steep correlation between the concentration of hdl and the risk of coronary heart disease (chd). hdl protects ldl against oxidation, an effect that persists for at least eight hours more durable and efficient than antioxidant vitamins. the antioxidant action is due to the enzyme paraoxonase. patients with acute chest pain or angiographically proven chd have half the paraoxonase activity seen in controls. a prospective study on men in south wales showed that serum paraoxonase activity is inversely correlated with the risk of chd. the activity is affected by genetic polymorphism: rr homozygotes have a 50% greater risk of chd. it is proposed that hdl evolved to protect cell membranes against oxidation. from the outside, ldl particles look like cell membranes, so the beneficial effect of hdl paraoxonase on ldl oxidation may be fortuitous. professor paul holvoet, university of leuven, belgium professor paul holvoet discussed the anti-inflammatory properties of hdl, again focussing on paraoxonase. he described studies on genetically modified mice, showing that human-like hdl reduced the oxidative stress observed in mice lacking the gene for apolipoprotein e. the inflammatory mediator, platelet-activating factor (paf), had a similar effect. professor holvoet proposed that paf is associated with the hdl particle; an increase in either leads to lower levels of oxidised ldl. the apoe-deficient mouse is an acceptable model of hypercholesterolaemia but it does not show symptoms of the metabolic syndrome, e.g. obesity. leptin-deficient (ob/ob) mice are a good model for obesity, insulin resistance and diabetes but do not develop atherosclerosis. professor holvoet has crossed the ob ob mice with ldl receptor-deficient mice, which develop atherosclerosis when fed an atherogenic diet. the double mutants, on a standard diet, show symptoms of the metabolic syndrome associated with accelerated atherosclerosis, such as increased macrophage homing. they also show higher plasma paf-acetyl hydrolase activity but this is associated with ldl not hdl and may be atherogenic. paraoxonase and lecithin:cholesterol acetyltransferase (lcat) activity are both reduced in these obese dyslipidaemic mice; introduction of the lcat gene partially prevents atherosclerosis in the absence of a change in hdl cholesterol level. when the mice were put on a starvation diet, they showed significant weight loss due to reduced fat accumulation, with a decrease in triglyceride concentrations and a change in ldl type. the relevance of this work was corroborated by measuring the levels of circulating oxidised ldl in patients these increased with the degree of individual metabolic syndrome abnormalities. dr roger newton, esperion therapeutics, michigan, usa dr roger newton introduced the clinical applications of these scientific studies with his company's work on hdl therapies. an unstable atherosclerotic plaque contains foam cells that secrete factors that attract macrophages and lead to rupture. these plaques have not yet impinged on the lumen and therefore cannot be treated via angioplasty. the aim is to mobilise the lipid core/cholesterol to prevent build up of plaque. dr newton listed three possible approaches: using a drug to raise the concentration of hdl and augment the effects of statins; using a cholesterol sponge , comprising an empty liposome made of synthetic phospholipids; or using an hdl mimetic. infusion of hdl particles can mobilise cholesterol and induce changes in vascular function and structure. large unilamellar liposomes have been shown to mobilise half their own weight in cholesterol and a recent efficacy study in humans showed a reduction in plaque volume after five weeks of treatment. the allelic variant apoa-1 milano protects human carriers against vascular disease. it facilitates hdl transport back to the liver and stabilises plaques in cholesterol-fed rabbits. a peptide mimetic of apoa1 enhances cholesterol efflux and is currently in phase 1 trials. dr vanessa rodie, glasgow royal infirmary, uk dr vanessa rodie gave the sue mccarthy travelling scholarship lecture, reporting on her work in australia with barbara meyer on the relationship between maternal insulin resistance/dyslipidaemia and maternal and fetal membrane fatty acid composition. insulin resistance is central to the development of pre-eclampsia. dr rodie found that pre-eclampsic pregnancies affected the maternal erythrocyte membrane fatty acid composition but not that of the fetus. dr john chapman, hopital de la pitie, paris, france the myant lecture was given by dr john chapman on inflammation, bioactive lipids and atherosclerosis. he gave an excellent overview of the many contradictory studies in this area. accelerated atherosclerosis results from a constellation of risk factors that have synergistic effects, e.g. hypertension, diabetes, obesity. the two most common risk factors in the uk and france are atherogenic dyslipidaemia and hypertension. both act on the arterial wall, leading to endothelial dysfunction, inflammation and oxidative stress. macrophage foam cells accumulate at the site of lesions; they contain cholesterol derived from ldl in the circulation. oxidative stress acts on arterial lipoproteins leading to inflammation and this activity is enhanced by bioactive lipids, many of which are found in plaques, e.g. paf, oxidised phospholipids and oxidised cholesterol esters. some of these are substrates for secretory phospholipase a2 and paf-acetyl hydrolase the two most common phospholipases in the circulation. it is not clear whether the net activity of these enzymes is pro- or anti-inflammatory. phospholipase a2 hydrolyses glycerophospholipids of lipoproteins and cell membranes. its expression is upregulated in inflammatory conditions and it is implicated in atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease. it potentiates the binding of phosphoglycerides and arterial retention of dense ldl and decreases hdl activity. paf-acetyl hydrolase (paf-ah) is more controversial, with contradictory results from in vivo and in vitro studies. it is glycosylated by macrophages, kupfer cells and platelets and the degree of glycosylation determines whether it associates with hdl or ldl. it is mainly bound to small dense ldl, which may facilitate access to hydrophobic lipid substrates and enhance catalytic efficiency. elevated paf-ah activity is associated with high ldl levels in familial hypercholesterolaemia. epidemiological studies have shown that high plasma paf-ah is a strong independent risk factor for chd in hypercholesterolaemic men (woscops) and is significantly associated with chd risk (the women's health study). is this causal or a consequence? abuzeid et al. 1 demonstrated that genetically attenuated paf-ah activity is associated with reduced chd risk and concluded that the enzyme has a proinflammatory role. statins reduced ldl-associated paf-ah activity in hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia but hdl-associated paf-ah and paraoxonase activities were unchanged. surprisingly, fenofibrate reduced paf-ah activity associated with atherogenic apob-containing lipoproteins but induced hdl-associated paf-ah activity, suggesting that statins and fibrates affect hdl particle phenotype in distinct ways. a complicating factor is that some of these changes could be due to paraoxonase. dr chapman summarised by saying that paf-ah exerts anti-inflammatory antiatherogenic actions on hdl, although these may be due to paraoxonase, while the jury is still out regarding ldl. possible therapeutic targets are paf-ah associated with dense ldl and the attenuation of oxidative stress and inflammatory stimuli in patients at high global cardiovascular risk. professor paul durrington, university of manchester, uk the second day was opened by professor paul durrington discussing the properties of ldl. the concentration of serum apolipoprotein b (apob) varies in different types of hyperlipidaemia. each particle contains one apob molecule so measuring apob indicates the number of particles as well as the concentration. ldl size also varies: people with low plasma triglyceride and high hdl-cholesterol have predominantly smaller particles. can ldl particle size be used as a prognostic factor for coronary artery disease? measurement of apob is a better risk indicator than measurement of ldl or serum cholesterol, but as statin therapy lowers the threshold for treatment, apob assays become relatively expensive for the number of people they identify as being at risk. professor durrington has developed a simple centrifuge method for measuring small dense ldl that he would like to introduce into clinical trials and ultimately into routine clinical practice. dr nick finer, addenbrooke's hospital, cambridge, uk dr nick finer returned to the subject of obesity and cardiovascular risk. one interesting observation was the importance of cuff size when measuring blood pressure; he pointed out that the majority of diabetic patients should be assessed using a large cuff, which is often not the case. the framingham study showed an increase in mortality due to obesity, with a 5% increase in risk of heart failure for men for a one point increase in bmi. a similar increase in relative risk was seen in the nurses' study in both diabetic and non-diabetic patients. the american heart association has upgraded obesity to a full risk factor for chd. the metabolic profiles of obese men were similar for those with low visceral fat to the lean group, while high visceral fat was associated with poor metabolic indicators. visceral fat has several components that affect chd risk; for example, changes in sympathetic nervous activity alter heart function, leading to high blood pressure, which in turn causes adverse effects on the left ventricle resulting in eccentric hypertrophy. left ventricular hypertrophy is a major risk factor for heart failure. weight loss reduces cardiovascular risk directly through effects on hypertension and dyslipidaemia and indirectly through a reduced risk of diabetes. moderate weight loss induced physiologically has a major effect on risk factors, whereas major weight loss caused by surgery has only a minor impact over 10 years of follow-up. a problem is that many patients regain any weight lost, which confounds studies on the effects of acute weight loss. dr finer studied a group of people subjected to a strict diet for eight weeks. over time, they regained some weight, but less fat. the best predictor of metabolic improvement at one year was waist circumference, even compared with careful measurements of body fat. dr finer concluded by saying that the management of obesity should be integral to the management of hypertension and cardiovascular risk. professor christopher byrne, university of southampton, uk there was a parallel session on metabolic syndrome and childhood obesity organised by the health care section. the metabolic syndrome was covered by professor chris byrne. insulin resistance is a huge problem that is driving an epidemic of type 2 diabetes; however, he emphasised that the metabolic syndrome is highly heterogeneous. professor byrne referred to harry keen's poisoned fruits of insulin resistance: the fruits are chd, hypertension, obesity, type 2 diabetes and dyslipidaemia. the tree's roots are the predisposing factors, such as food, early development, physical inactivity and genetics. obesity is a relatively recent phenomenon and is itself heterogeneous in development and manifestation we see pear-shaped women and apple-shaped men. not everybody with obesity has the metabolic syndrome. professor byrne is studying gene expression in three groups of men, grouped by body mass, with and without the metabolic syndrome. he has found that glucocorticoid receptor expression is inversely associated with insulin sensitivity and he will continue to investigate a range of genes involved in fat metabolism. the maths presented made it all seem simple. the brain and red blood cells need 180 g carbohydrate per day. gluconeogenesis generates 130 g, therefore dietary glucose needs to provide only 50 g. our muscle and glycogen stores contain 500 700 g carbohydrate, which is depleted over about 12 hours. however, we keep replenishing these stores before they are empty and the excess glucose has to be turned into fat. professor byrne does not believe that the glycaemic index is very important because all carbohydrates end up as glucose molecules, only the speed varies. heart uk 7 north road, maidenhead, berkshire sl6 1pe. title: ldl density and oxidation are modulated by pon1 promoter genotype in patients with alzheimer's disease
display_name: LDL Density and Oxidation are Modulated by PON1 Promoter Genotype in Patients with Alzheimer's Disease
abstract: cholesterol metabolism alteration is a hot topic in the field of alzheimer's disease (ad). however, data on plasma lipoproteins cholesterol distribution and oxidation in ad and their possible genetic determinants are lacking. the paraoxonase-1 (pon1) gene -107c/t promoter polymorphisms have been found associated with ad. one of the fundamental functions of pon1 enzyme is the inhibition of low-density lipoproteins (ldl) oxidation. we therefore evaluated plasma lipoprotein profile and ldl density and oxidation in late-onset ad patients and healthy elderly subjects, without neuroimaging evidence of cerebrovascular lesions and not on lipid-lowering treatment, and their interaction with pon1 -107c/t and apolipoprotein e (apoe) genotypes. mean plasma total cholesterol and ldl levels were higher in ad than controls (p < 0.05). lipoproteins cholesterol distribution shifted toward a greater prevalence of smaller, denser ldl (sd-ldl, p < 0.05) only in ad patients with pon1 -107tt genotype, who also showed increased plasma levels of oxidized ldl (ox-ldl, p = 0.02). a significant association was observed between sd-ldl and ox-ldl levels (p < 005) in ad patients. apoe genotype did not modulate lipoprotein distribution. increased levels of sd-ldl and ox-ldl particles in the ad pon1 tt patients could be explained by the combined effect of an ad-related pro-oxidant milieu and an ineffective pon1 gene polymorphism-related antioxidant capacity. the functional correlate of the association between pon1 -107c/t polymorphism and ad may be the abnormal modulation of ldl oxidation. ox-ldl may amplify the processes of endothelial injury promoted by vascular amyloid deposition, which represents one of the potential pathways explaining the cross-road between vascular and neurodegenerative pathomechanisms in ad.

title: reduced progression of atherosclerosis in apolipoprotein e deficient mice following consumption of red wine, or its polyphenols quercetin or catechin, is associated with reduced susceptibility of ldl to oxidation and aggregation

abstract: abstract the effect of consuming red wine, or its major polyphenol constituents catechin or quercetin, on the development of atherosclerotic lesions, in relation to the susceptibility of plasma ldl to oxidation and to aggregation, was studied in atherosclerotic apolipoprotein e deficient (e ) mice. forty e mice at the age of 4 weeks were divided into four groups, 10 mice in each group, and were supplemented for up to 6 weeks in their drinking water with placebo (1.1% alcohol); catechin or quercetin (50 g/d per mouse), or red wine (0.5 ml/d per mouse). consumption of catechin, quercetin, or red wine had no effect on plasma ldl or hdl cholesterol levels. the atherosclerotic lesion area was smaller in the treated mice by 39%, 46%, and 48%, respectively, in comparison with e mice that were treated with placebo. in accordance with these findings, cellular uptake of ldl derived after catechin, quercetin, or red wine consumption was found to be reduced by 31%, 40%, and 52%, respectively. these results were associated with reduced susceptibility to oxidation (induced by different modes such as copper ions, free radical generator, or macrophages) of ldl isolated after red wine or quercetin and, to a lesser extent after catechin consumption, in comparison with ldl isolated from the placebo group. similar results were obtained when ldl was preincubated in vitro with red wine or with the polyphenols prior to its oxidation. even in the basal oxidative state (not induced oxidation), ldl isolated from e mice that consumed catechin, quercetin, or red wine for 2 weeks was found to be less oxidized in comparison with ldl isolated from e mice that received placebo, as evidenced by 39%, 48%, and 49% reduced content of ldl-associated lipid peroxides, respectively. this effect could be related to enhanced serum paraoxonase activity in the polyphenol-treated mice. ldl oxidation was previously shown to lead to its aggregation. the present study demonstrated that the susceptibility of ldl to aggregation was reduced in comparison with placebo-treated mice, by 63%, 48%, or 50% by catechin, quercetin, and red wine consumption, respectively, and this effect could be shown also in vitro. the inhibition of ldl oxidation by polyphenols could be related, at least in part, to a direct effect of the polyphenols on the ldl, since both quercetin and catechin were found to bind to the ldl particle via the formation of an ether bond. we thus conclude that dietary consumption by e mice of red wine or its polyphenolic flavonoids quercetin and, to a lesser extent, catechin leads to attenuation in the development of the atherosclerotic lesion, and this effect is associated with reduced susceptibility of their ldl to oxidation and aggregation.

title: a catalog of human genes associated with pathozoospermia and functional characteristics of these genes
display_name: A Catalog of Human Genes Associated With Pathozoospermia and Functional Characteristics of These Genes
abstract: genetic causes of the global decline in male fertility are among the hot spots of scientific research in reproductive genetics. the most common way to evaluate male fertility in clinical trials is to determine semen quality. lower semen quality is very often accompanied by subfertility or infertility, occurs in many diseases and can be caused by many factors, including genetic ones. the following forms of lowered semen quality (pathozoospermia) are known: azoospermia, oligozoospermia, asthenozoospermia, teratozoospermia, and some combined forms. to systematize information about the genetic basis of impaired spermatogenesis, we created a catalog of human genes associated with lowered semen quality (hgapat) and analyzed their functional characteristics. the catalog comprises data on 126 human genes. each entry of the catalog describes an association between an allelic variant of the gene and a particular form of lowered semen quality, extracted from the experimental study. most genes included into the catalog are located on autosomes and are associated with such pathologies as non-obstructive azoospermia, oligozoospermia or asthenozoospermia. slightly less than half of the included genes (43%) are expressed in the testes in a tissue-specific manner. functional annotation of genes from the catalog showed that spermatogenic failure can be associated with mutations in genes that control biological processes essential for spermiogenesis (regulating dna metabolism, cell division, formation of cellular structures, which provide cell movement) as well as with mutations in genes that control cellular responses to unfavorable conditions (stress factors, including oxidative stress and exposure to toxins).

title: activity of paraoxonase 1 (pon1) and its relationship to markers of lipoprotein oxidation in healthy slovaks.
display_name: Activity of paraoxonase 1 (PON1) and its relationship to markers of lipoprotein oxidation in healthy Slovaks.
abstract: low-density lipoproteins (ldls), when modified by free radicals derived from artery wall cells, induce atherosclerosis. in contrast to oxidized ldl (ox-ldl), high-density lipoproteins (hdls) are able to prevent atherosclerosis through a protein with antioxidant properties, paraoxonase 1 (pon1). the purpose of this study was to explore the association between the activity of hdl-associated pon1 and circulating ox-ldl as well as to investigate the relationship between ox-ldl and parameters of lipid profile in thirty slovaks aged 21-73 years because recent studies have presented controversial results concerning pon1 and its role in ldl oxidation. for determination of circulating ox-ldl sandwich elisa was used and other lipid parameters were determined by routine laboratory analyses. pon1 activities were assayed by two synthetic substrates - paraoxon and phenyl acetate. lipid peroxides were determined spectrophotometrically. of the lipid parameters examined, ox-ldl level correlated positively with total (p < 0.0001) and ldl-cholesterol (p < 0.001). triacylglycerols (tag) (p < 0.001), lipid peroxides (p < 0.01) and atherogenic index (ai = total cholesterol/hdl) (p < 0.0001) were also strongly correlated with ox-ldl. no inverse relationships were observed between ox-ldl and hdl-cholesterol or arylesterase/paraoxonase activities of pon1. furthermore, it was found that ox-ldl (p < 0.01) and lipid peroxides (p < 0.05) were significantly higher in men than in women. pon1 arylesterase activity was marginally affected by sex. the results of this study suggest that the anti-atherogenic properties of hdls are not directly related to their total concentration and that pon1 activity determined towards synthetic compounds (paraoxon and phenyl acetate) reflects no association with markers of oxidative stress. furthermore, it follows from our results that men are more susceptible to developing atherosclerosis compared to women.

title: metabolites in the regulatory risk assessment of pesticides in the eu
display_name: Metabolites in the regulatory risk assessment of pesticides in the EU

authorships.name: Gerrit Wolterink
institutions: National Institute for Public Health and the Environment

abstract: a large majority of chemicals is converted into metabolites through xenobiotic-metabolising enzymes. metabolites may present a spectrum of characteristics varying from similar to vastly different compared with the parent compound in terms of both toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics. in the pesticide arena, the role of metabolism and metabolites is increasingly recognised as a significant factor particularly for the design and interpretation of mammalian toxicological studies and in the toxicity assessment of pesticide/metabolite-associated issues for hazard characterization and risk assessment purposes, including the role of metabolites as parts in various residues in ecotoxicological adversities. this is of particular relevance to pesticide metabolites that are unique to humans in comparison with metabolites found in in vitro or in vivo animal studies, but also to disproportionate metabolites (quantitative differences) between humans and mammalian species. presence of unique or disproportionate metabolites may underlie potential toxicological concerns. this review aims to present the current state-of-the-art of comparative metabolism and metabolites in pesticide research for hazard and risk assessment, including one health perspectives, and future research needs based on the experiences gained at the european food safety authority.
